content: The systematic review conducted by Lana Chikhungu, Stephanie Bispo, and Marie-Louise Newell focused on postnatal HIV transmission rates at six and 12 months of age in infants born to HIV-infected mothers who were on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and initiated breastfeeding. The 2010 WHO guidelines on infant feeding in the context of HIV recommended exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for the first six months, followed by complementary feeding and continued breastfeeding (CBF) for up to one year, provided either the mother or infant was on ART. However, at the time these guidelines were developed, there was limited data on the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in women who were on ART during pregnancy and continued ART postpartum, or in infants receiving ART prophylaxis for prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). Over the past five years, additional evidence has emerged from studies and programs that achieved postnatal PMTCT through maternal ART or infant antiretroviral (ARV) prophylaxis. A key question remains regarding the potential increased risk of HIV transmission when infants receive mixed feeding (breast milk combined with other feeds) during the first six months of life, as this practice was previously associated with a significantly higher risk of transmission in the pre-ART and pre-PMTCT era. In October 2015, the WHO guidelines on HIV and infant feeding were reviewed in light of the expanded use of ART in pregnant and breastfeeding women. This systematic review aimed to address whether maternal ART is effective in reducing the risk of postnatal HIV transmission, even when mothers practice mixed feeding. The review included data from randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and longitudinal studies involving HIV-positive mothers on ART and their breastfed infants. Infants may also have received prophylactic ARVs as per the 2010 WHO guidelines. The search strategy involved multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and CINAHL, covering studies published between 2005 and 2015. Conference abstracts from the International AIDS Society (IAS) and the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) were also reviewed. A total of 1,439 citations were identified, of which 11 studies met the inclusion criteria after screening and full-text review. The included studies primarily involved HIV-positive mothers who initiated ART before or during pregnancy and continued ART for at least six months postpartum. Eight studies followed the WHO recommendation of six-month ART, while three studies provided lifelong ART to all mothers or only to those eligible for treatment based on low CD4 counts. The review found that six studies reported HIV transmission rates at six months, while five studies reported transmission rates beyond six months. The overall transmission rates varied across studies, with some reporting rates as low as 1% to 2% at six months. However, there was considerable heterogeneity in the reported rates, and some studies lacked detailed data on feeding practices or maternal adherence to ART. Mixed feeding was not consistently analyzed as a separate risk factor for transmission, and most studies assumed that mothers exclusively breastfed their infants for the first six months. The pooled analysis of transmission rates revealed significant variability, with confidence intervals calculated for studies that did not provide them. The review highlighted the need for more robust data on the impact of mixed feeding on postnatal HIV transmission in the context of maternal ART. Additionally, the quality of evidence was rated as very low due to study limitations, inconsistency, and indirectness of the research questions relative to the primary objectives of the review. In conclusion, while maternal ART significantly reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission, the evidence on the impact of mixed feeding remains limited and inconsistent. Further research is needed to clarify the relationship between feeding practices and transmission risk, particularly in settings where ART is widely available.
